title: C strings: the byte at the end

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own lesson text and examples on c strings: the byte at the end, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can explain how C knows where a string ends
can tell strlen from sizeof and predict both
can read and copy strings without writing past a buffer

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: C has no string type. A "string" is just bytes in a `char` array, ending with a byte whose value is 0. That one convention explains a huge share of C bugs, from off-by-one buffer sizes to the overflows behind famous security holes. Interviewers use it to check whether you understand memory, not just syntax.

sections.heading: A string is bytes plus a 0
sections.body:
The literal `"chai"` is five bytes: `'c' 'h' 'a' 'i' '\0'`. The last one, the **null terminator** (value 0), marks the end. Every string function, from `printf("%s")` to `strlen` and `strcpy`, walks forward until it finds that 0. **C never stores a string's length; it finds it by searching.**

Two sizes now matter, and they are different:

- `strlen(s)`: the number of characters **before** the terminator. It walks the bytes, so it costs `O(n)`.
- `sizeof buf`: the size of the **whole array** in bytes, known at compile time, including the terminator and any unused space after it.

A buffer must have room for the terminator: storing a 7-letter word needs at least 8 bytes.

> **Note:** `char word[] = "chai";` lets the compiler count, and it allocates 5 bytes. `char word[4] = "chai";` compiles in C but leaves **no room for the terminator**, so `word` is not a valid string. This is one of the places C and C++ differ: C++ rejects it.

sections.heading: strlen, sizeof and the terminator
sections.body: The array `hostel` has 16 bytes but holds a 6-letter word. Writing a 0 into the middle shortens the string without changing the array.

code.expected_output:
strlen = 6, sizeof = 16
byte after the last letter = 0
sizeof word = 5 (4 letters + the terminator)
after hostel[3] = 0: "Kav", strlen = 3
code.caption: strlen counts up to the terminator; sizeof counts the whole buffer

sections.heading: Reading and copying without overflowing
sections.body:
The dangerous functions are the ones that **do not know the destination's size**:

- `gets(buf)` reads a whole line no matter how long; it was removed from the C standard. Use `fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin)`, which writes at most `sizeof buf − 1` characters plus the terminator.
- `strcpy(dst, src)` copies until `src` ends, even past the end of `dst`. Prefer `snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src)`, which always terminates and never writes more than `sizeof dst` bytes; its return value tells you how long the full string would have been, so you can detect truncation.
- `scanf("%s", buf)` has the same problem; give it a width: `scanf("%31s", buf)` for a 32-byte buffer.

`fgets` keeps the newline if the line fit. `line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0';` removes it: `strcspn` returns the index of the first newline, or the length if there is none, so the line is safe either way.

sections.heading: A safe read and a safe copy
sections.body: The program reads `Narmada Hostel` from standard input, strips the newline, and copies it into an 8-byte `tag`. `snprintf` keeps 7 characters and the terminator; nothing is written past the buffer.

code.expected_output:
read "Narmada Hostel" (14 chars)
tag  "Narmada" (cut to fit 8 bytes)
code.caption: Reading a line safely and copying it into a smaller buffer

sections.heading: What an overflow actually does
sections.body:
Suppose a function has `char name[8];` followed by other local variables, and calls `strcpy(name, input)` with a 20-character input. The first 8 bytes fill `name`; the next 12 overwrite **whatever lives next to it in memory**: another variable, a saved pointer, or the return address of the function. The program may print a wrong value, crash much later in unrelated code, or, if an attacker chose the input, jump to code the attacker supplied. This is the classic **stack buffer overflow**.

Notice that nothing fails at the moment of the bad write. That is what makes these bugs expensive: the symptom appears far from the cause. Two habits prevent almost all of them: **every write into a buffer passes the buffer's size** (`fgets`, `snprintf`, `strncat` with care), and **every buffer is sized for the terminator**. When testing, `-fsanitize=address` reports the exact overflowing line instead of a random crash later.

sections.heading: Walking a string with a pointer
sections.body:
The hands-on task asks you to count vowels by walking the string yourself. The standard C shape is:

```c
for (const char *p = s; *p != '\0'; p++) {
    /* look at *p */
}
```

The loop stops on the terminator, so it never needs the length. Compare it with the tempting version `for (size_t i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++)`: it is correct, but `strlen` walks the whole string **on every iteration**, so a loop over `n` characters does about `n^2 / 2` steps. On a 200-character line nobody notices; on a 2 MB file it takes seconds instead of milliseconds. If you need the length, compute it once before the loop.

Two more details for the task:

- **Case:** `tolower` from `<ctype.h>` turns `'A'` into `'a'` and leaves other characters alone. Pass it an `unsigned char` value: `tolower((unsigned char)*p)`. A plain `char` can be negative for non-ASCII bytes (such as UTF-8 letters in Hindi text), and passing a negative value to `tolower` is undefined behaviour.
- **The newline:** `fgets` keeps the `'\n'`. It is not a vowel, so it would not change the count here, but stripping it is a good habit: the moment you compare the line with another string, or print it inside quotes, a stray newline gives a wrong answer.

Trace `"Chai Point"`: C (no), h (no), a (1), i (2), space, P, o (3), i (4), n, t. The answer is 4, and the loop stopped at the terminator after `t` without ever asking how long the line was.

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think `strlen` includes the terminator.** It does not: `strlen("chai")` is 4. The buffer needs `strlen + 1` bytes.

**Many students think `sizeof` gives the string's length.** It gives the array's size, which is often larger, and for a `char *` parameter it gives the pointer's size (8), which has nothing to do with the text.

**Many students think `strncpy` is the safe `strcpy`.** If the source is too long, `strncpy` copies exactly `n` bytes and **does not add a terminator**, leaving an unterminated string. `snprintf` is the simpler safe choice.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.q: How does `printf("%s", s)` know where the string ends?
qa.a: It reads bytes from s until it finds a byte with value 0, the null terminator. C stores no length, so a missing terminator makes printf run past the buffer into other memory.

qa.q: What is the difference between `strlen(s)` and `sizeof s` for `char s[20] = "hi";`?
qa.a: strlen is 2, the characters before the terminator, found by scanning. sizeof is 20, the size of the whole array, known at compile time. For a char pointer, sizeof would be the pointer size instead.

qa.q: Why was `gets` removed from the C standard?
qa.a: It reads an entire line into a buffer without knowing the buffer's size, so any long input overflows it. There is no way to use it safely; fgets with the buffer size replaces it.

qa.q: How would you copy a string into a fixed buffer safely?
qa.a: snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src): it never writes more than the buffer size, always adds the terminator, and returns the length the full string needed, so I can check for truncation.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- A C string is a `char` array ending in a 0 byte.
- `strlen` scans to the terminator; `sizeof` is the whole buffer.
- Buffers need `length + 1` bytes.
- Use functions that take the destination size: `fgets`, `snprintf`.
- Overflows corrupt neighbouring memory silently; sanitisers find them.

Which call can never write past `char buf[16]`?
quiz.explanation: snprintf is told the buffer size and always terminates.

hands_on.title: Count the vowels
hands_on.task: Read one line (at most 200 characters) and print how many of its letters are vowels (`a e i o u`, upper or lower case). Fill in `count_vowels`, walking the string with a pointer until you reach the `'\0'` terminator. Do not use `strlen` in the loop condition.

revision_card.front: C strings: how is the end found, strlen vs sizeof, and the safe read and copy?
revision_card.back: A 0 byte ends every string; C stores no length. strlen counts chars before it; sizeof is the whole buffer. Read with fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin); copy with snprintf(dst, sizeof dst, "%s", src).
